# Nebius raises GPU list prices up to 21% while H100 spot sits at $0.79

October 22, 2026

By

CTOL Staff Reporter

Table Of Contents

- What changed in the price list
- What the live spot market shows
- Benchmarks for a GPU rental contract

Posted prices for four Nebius GPU types rose 17 to 21 percent on 1 October. Its own spot board shows Blackwell chips near 60 percent of list and an H100 at the floor, so the squeeze sits in particular chips and regions.

Nebius told CNBC this week that AI computing prices are rising faster than it expected. On 1 October it lifted the posted price of four GPU types by 17 to 21 percent. Anyone renting GPUs has to decide whether that posted price is what they will pay.

The posted price mostly is not what buyers pay. It rose, but the price at which capacity actually clears is uneven, and Nebius now publishes it. Scarcity is specific to Blackwell chips and some regions, while older H100 capacity is sitting idle.

### What changed in the price list

The Nebius pricing documentation dates two changes. The first took effect on 1 October, when on demand prices per GPU hour rose for four chips. Reuters reported on 17 September that Nebius had announced it, its second price rise in three months.

- B300 went from $7.85 to $9.50, up 21.0 percent, the largest rise.
- B200 went from $7.15 to $8.50, up 18.9 percent.
- H200 went from $4.50 to $5.40, up 20.0 percent.
- H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50, up 16.9 percent, the smallest rise of the four.

The RTX PRO 6000 stayed at $1.80, so the rise did not reach every GPU.

The second change came on 8 October. The preemptible tier, which rents interruptible capacity at a discount, stopped using fixed prices. It moved to dynamic spot pricing that can change every 15 minutes.

One rule in the documentation matters most. The highest spot price is always one cent below the current on demand rate, so the new list price is a ceiling. The floor is $0.79 or $0.99 depending on the chip. The posted price rise matters to a spot buyer only when the market pushes against that ceiling.

### What the live spot market shows

On 21 October Nebius announced public live spot pricing, also shown on Shadeform, Silicon Data and GPU Finder. Nebius's spot board shows how far below the ceiling each chip sits. At 23:03 UTC on Wednesday, B300 cleared at $5.29 to $5.89 across three regions, 56 to 62 percent of list.

B200 cleared at $4.40 and $4.50, which is 52 and 53 percent of list. Across five Blackwell regions, then, spot cleared at 52 to 62 percent of list. That is 38 to 48 percent below the posted price, well above the floor, and still far under the ceiling.

H200 prices split sharply by region. In eu-north1 it cleared at $2.00, 37 percent of the $5.40 list. In eu-west1 it cleared at $5.09, 94 percent, so one chip showed a spread of 2.5 times between two regions.

H100 trades at the floor. It trades at $0.79 in eu-north1, its only region, and has done since 9 October at 17:01 UTC. Across the 12 markets on the board, the median spot price is about 57 percent of list.

Spot prices did not rise across the board. Live spot is between 63 percent below and 108 percent above the old fixed preemptible prices. Blackwell spot is above the old fixed prices, and H100 spot is far below them.

B300 and B200 are up 11 to 37 percent. H200 ranges from 18 percent lower to 108 percent higher. H100 is 63 percent lower.

The chart shows two markets sharing one price list. Blackwell, at 52 to 62 percent of list, and the eu-west1 H200, at 94 percent, clear highest against the ceiling. High clearing prices are what scarcity looks like. H100 and the Finnish H200 clear near the floor, which is what slack looks like.

The board is also noisy. The B300 price in eu-west2 fell 44 percent in a day. The Finnish H200 rose 82 percent. Both are one day moves, so this Wednesday evening UTC snapshot is a position, not a trend.

Nebius's revenue chief says prices keep rising, and the board does not contradict him for Blackwell. CNBC reported that Nebius's chief revenue officer said an auction on Tuesday showed continued price rises. His metric was price per megawatt, not GPU hours, and he agreed it kept rising.

The same executive said supply continues to fall far behind demand, and that 2027 capacity would sell out if it came online. Auctions and long commitments are a different market from interruptible spot capacity. The board shows the same business from the cheap end.

His case is weaker for H100 than for Blackwell. An H100 at $0.79 for 12 days is a data point against "supply falls far behind demand". It covers one chip in the only region that offers it. The posted price rise is not what a flexible buyer paid on Wednesday.

Nebius also said it is piloting a capacity rebate programme. Customers can recover value by releasing idle GPUs back into the spot pool. A scheme like that matters only if some GPUs sit idle.

Crusoe's on demand H200 and H100 sit below Nebius's list. Its pricing page lists on demand H200 at $4.29 an hour, 21 percent under Nebius's posted price. H100 is $3.90, and B300 is $9.90 against $9.50 at Nebius.

Crusoe's chief executive, Chase Lochmiller, still told CNBC that A100 pricing is higher than in 2020 or 2021. He said H100 pricing is higher than when those chips were first deployed in 2023.

### Benchmarks for a GPU rental contract

A reserved H200 rate should be compared with $5.40 on demand at Nebius, $4.29 at Crusoe and a live spot range of $2.00 to $5.09.

A rate near the posted price would pay for scarcity that the board shows in only some places. A training run that tolerates interruption can bid near the floor on H100 or Finnish H200. A run that needs Blackwell in a given week should expect to pay 52 to 62 percent of list.

An H100 clearing at $0.79 against a $4.50 list price is also the first live test of residual value for an older GPU fleet. That means what the equipment is still worth. The price is posted openly and refreshes as often as every 15 minutes.

The test of the price rise is whether spot prices drift toward the new ceiling over the coming weeks. On 21 October they had not.

List price only bites where buyers push spot up to it, and the H100 floor shows where they have not. When Nebius next reports, the realised price per GPU hour on H100 and H200 will show whether the $0.79 floor was 12 days of slack or a trend.
